newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions, employers seek sick pay compromise.
newsitem.headline: German unions, employers seek sick pay compromise.

text.p: Klaus Zwickel, chairman of the German trade union IG Metall, said on Monday he was entering an emergency meeting with employers to discuss plans to cut sick pay with "no great expectations" of a quick agreement.

Metals and electronics union IG Metall and the employers' union Gesamtmetall were meeting to discuss sick pay after attempts last week by major firms to implement a controversial law cutting benefits were met by mass protests.

"When you consider that 150,000 workers in the metal industry last week protested over this, it shows the level of indignation and rage that workers feel over this. In such a situation any solution will be complicated," Zwickel said,
Speaking to journalists as he arrived for the meeting, Zwickel added that the union had "no interest in the situation escalating".
IG Metall vice-chairman Walter Riester, also arriving for the talks, re-affirmed that the union would only be talking about the issue of cuts in sick pay, rather than wider pay talks.

Employer representatives denied weekend news reports that the meeting had been requested by German industrial giant Daimler-Benz AG, which was the first large company to introduce the cuts and has already been hit by wildcat strikes.
Dieter Hundt, vice president of Gesamtmetall said employers had "for weeks" been inviting IG Metall to discuss a new law seeking to trim sick pay costs by 20 percent.

"The metal and electronics industry does not need a hot autumn but cool heads," Hundt told German radio on Monday, referring to the "hot autumn" of industrial unrest that many union leaders have been threatening.
IG Metall vice chairman Walter Riester said at the weekend that Germany would see "tougher strikes than the country has ever experienced" if no agreement can be reached on the matter.
The talks are taking place at a hotel just outside of Frankfurt and a statement from the two sides is expected at around 1500 GMT.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday repeated calls for the two sides to debate the issue sensibly and criticised them for not having attempted to reach a consensus earlier.

Employers and unions are seen as initially seeking to defuse tension on the issue, particularly with IG Metall due to announce its overall 1997 wage demands for the 3.5 million workers it represents on Tuesday.

Further protests are also being planned at Daimler for Thursday to follow the stoppages involving around 100,000 Daimler employees last Tuesday that were estimated to have cost Daimler's Mercedes luxury car unit alone 80 million marks ($52 million).
